title: Pennsylvania Measles Deaths Rise to Nine as Cases Reach 1,638
excerpt: An unvaccinated Centre County resident is the state's ninth measles-linked death this year; state departments count at least 13 deaths nationally while the CDC has confirmed six.
body:
• Pennsylvania reported another measles-linked death on November 23 — an unvaccinated Centre County resident — taking the state's toll to nine this year, from eight last week.
  • Pennsylvania has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 330 hospitalizations, according to the state health department.
  • State health departments have reported at least 13 measles-associated deaths in the US this year, while the CDC has confirmed six; nationwide, 5,838 confirmed cases were reported as of November 19, CDC data show.
  • For readers in the US: two doses of the MMR vaccine are more than 97% effective against measles, according to UChicago Medicine — children are due a first dose after their first birthday and a second at ages 4 to 6.

Pennsylvania's health department on Monday, November 23 reported another death linked to this year's measles outbreak, taking the number of fatalities associated with the disease in the state to nine, from eight last week, Reuters reported.

The latest death involved an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central Pennsylvania who had tested positive for measles, the department said. The nine deaths this year involved residents of Centre, Clinton, Jefferson, Lancaster, Mifflin and Montour counties; Lancaster County accounted for three deaths and Jefferson County for two.

The state and national picture

Pennsylvania has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far this year, including 330 hospitalizations, according to the health department. The state is the centre of the largest US measles outbreak in decades.

Nationwide, 5,838 confirmed measles cases were reported this year as of November 19, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Virginia on Friday reported its first measles-associated death of 2026, involving a child; Wisconsin has reported two deaths and New York state one child death.

Why the death counts differ

Based on publicly reported state figures, at least 13 measles-associated deaths have been recorded in the US this year. The CDC, however, has confirmed only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026 and has not specified the states where they occurred.

Reuters reported that the discrepancy arose earlier this year after the CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures. The US Department of Health and Human Services said it was "saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania" and that the CDC has provided the state nearly $4 million in one-time emergency funding for response efforts in 2027.

Last week, the US lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization announced the withdrawal on November 17 because measles has continued to spread in the country for more than a year, according to UChicago Medicine.

"Most of the outbreaks of measles this year have been centered in counties where a lot of Amish and conservative Mennonites live."

— Kathryn Jacobsen, epidemiologist at the University of Richmond, to Reuters

Jacobsen added that large gatherings of unvaccinated people can allow the virus to spread rapidly, and that although the epidemic was currently centered in conservative, rural religious communities, other groups were also at risk.

What readers should do

Measles spreads through the air and through infectious droplets, and a person with measles is contagious from four days before the rash appears through four days after, UChicago Medicine notes. Symptoms — fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and then a rash — typically appear eight to 12 days after exposure.

Children should receive a first MMR dose after their first birthday and a second dose before kindergarten, at ages 4 to 6; an infant travelling internationally can receive a first dose as early as 6 months, which does not replace the later doses. Adults are considered immune if they have documentation of MMR vaccination, laboratory evidence of immunity or infection, or were born before 1957; adults who meet none of those criteria should be vaccinated. If you believe you have been exposed, UChicago Medicine advises wearing a mask, isolating, and calling your doctor before visiting a facility.
